results.summary: HIV-infected patients with bacterial meningitis may present atypically with normal or near-normal CSF cell counts due to impaired immune response, particularly with CD4 counts below 500 cells/mm3. Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common causative organism. Elevated CSF protein with low cell count (albuminocytologic dissociation) can occur and may be mistaken for non-infectious etiologies.
results.title: Bacterial Meningitis in HIV-Infected Patients: Atypical Presentations and Diagnostic Challenges

results.journal: Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes
results.summary: Pneumococcal meningitis remains the leading cause of bacterial meningitis in HIV-positive adults. Initial CSF may show blunted pleocytosis in immunosuppressed patients. Mortality is higher than in HIV-negative patients. Early empiric antibiotics with ceftriaxone and vancomycin plus dexamethasone remain the standard of care.
results.title: Pneumococcal Meningitis in the Setting of HIV Infection: Clinical Features and Outcomes

results.summary: Recurrent meningitis in HIV patients requires consideration of partially treated bacterial meningitis, cryptococcal meningitis, TB meningitis, neurosyphilis, and immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS). A systematic approach with comprehensive CSF testing including cultures, molecular diagnostics, and serologic markers is essential.
results.title: Recurrent Meningitis in HIV: Differential Diagnosis and Approach

prohibited_recommendations: Do NOT delay empiric antimicrobial therapy while awaiting imaging or LP results when bacterial meningitis is clinically suspected.
Do NOT perform lumbar puncture before CT head when any imaging-first criterion (altered mental status, focal deficit, papilledema, seizure, immunocompromise, age >60) is present.

Do NOT discontinue dexamethasone solely because the Gram stain is negative — completion of the 4-day course is appropriate in suspected pneumococcal meningitis until alternative organism is identified.
Do NOT rely on a negative Gram stain or a 'normal CT' to rule out bacterial meningitis when the clinical syndrome is present.
Do NOT treat with oral antibiotics alone; CNS penetration is inadequate for meningitis.
required_recommendations: Administer the first dose of empiric IV antibiotics (vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg + ceftriaxone 2 g) within 60 minutes of clinical suspicion; do NOT delay antibiotics for LP or imaging beyond what is strictly needed for safety.
Give adjunctive dexamethasone 10 mg IV before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue q6h for 4 days in confirmed pneumococcal meningitis.
Draw two sets of peripheral blood cultures before the first antibiotic dose.
Obtain CT head before LP because imaging-first criteria are present (altered mental status, immunocompromise, focal signs, papilledema, or age >60).
Send full CSF panel (cell count, differential, glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture, meningitis multiplex PCR, lactate) at the LP.
Reassess and de-escalate antibiotics based on Gram stain, culture, and susceptibility results.
Place patient on droplet precautions until meningococcal disease is excluded.
Confirm HIV status (CD4, viral load) and assess for opportunistic infections including cryptococcosis and TB.

avoided_actions.rationale: No evidence of endocarditis as a primary source in this case; echocardiography is not part of routine meningitis workup.
No arrhythmia indication; continuous cardiac monitoring contributes nothing to meningitis diagnosis or treatment.
PET imaging has no role in acute meningitis diagnosis; CT and MRI cover the indications.
Amyloid PET is a dementia biomarker tool with no role in acute infectious meningitis.

differential.key_features: Advanced HIV with prior empiric cryptococcal treatment 2 months ago — must rule out relapse with CrAg and culture
Lymphocyte-predominant CSF, normal-to-mildly elevated glucose, lower protein, lower CRP/procalcitonin — clinically distinguished by less toxic appearance

key_clinical_evidence: Acute bacterial meningitis presents with fever, headache, meningismus, and altered mental status; the full triad is present in only ~40%, so partial syndromes warrant aggressive workup.
Antibiotic timing matters: every hour of delay after the first hour increases mortality. Antibiotics MUST precede imaging or LP if either would delay treatment >60 minutes.
CT before LP is mandated when any imaging-first criterion is present (altered mental status, focal signs, papilledema, recent seizure, immunocompromise, or age >60).
Adjunctive dexamethasone (10 mg IV q6h × 4 days) given BEFORE or WITH the first antibiotic dose reduces mortality and unfavourable outcomes in pneumococcal meningitis (De Gans 2002, NEJM).
A negative CSF Gram stain (sensitivity ~60-90%, lower if antibiotic pretreated) does not exclude bacterial meningitis; multiplex PCR or antigen testing retains sensitivity.
CSF:serum glucose ratio <0.4 is more reliable than absolute CSF glucose for distinguishing bacterial from viral meningitis.
Empiric coverage must include vancomycin + ceftriaxone in adults; add ampicillin for Listeria coverage if age >50 or immunocompromised.
In advanced HIV, bacterial meningitis can present with pauci-cellular CSF; PCR-based and antigen-based diagnostics retain sensitivity when cellular response is blunted.
WHO 2025: obtain cultures promptly, but neither LP nor cranial imaging may delay empirical antimicrobials when the pathway requires treatment first.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Gram-stain sensitivity is only 60-90% even untreated; multiplex PCR and antigen testing must be used to confirm the organism.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Lower the index of suspicion for bacterial meningitis.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Humoral immunodeficiency (HIV, CVID) blunts the CSF inflammatory response; bacterial meningitis can present with pauci-cellular CSF, and PCR/antigen testing must be used.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggest viral or non-infectious aetiology rather than bacterial meningitis.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Parenchymal HIV-related lesions can coexist with acute bacterial meningitis; CSF Gram stain/PCR and culture identify the acute infection while the parenchymal lesion is worked up separately.
red_herrings.data_point: Subcortical white-matter lesion on MRI consistent with PML or low-grade glioma
red_herrings.intended_effect: Redirect workup toward chronic HIV-associated CNS disease and away from bacterial meningitis.

sequence_constraints.reason: Per IDSA 2004, non-contrast CT head must precede lumbar puncture whenever any imaging-first criterion is present (altered mental status, focal neurological deficit, papilledema, recent seizure, immunocompromise, or age >60). LP performed in undetected mass effect can precipitate fatal herniation.

metadata.condition_name: Acute bacterial meningitis (pneumococcal) in HIV-infected patient
metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle due to atypical CSF with albuminocytologic dissociation (high protein, near-normal cell count) in an immunocompromised host. Initial Gram stain and cultures are negative from prior antibiotic treatment. Red herrings include an oral ulcer suggesting neurosyphilis, behavioral changes mimicking HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder, and a right frontal lesion raising concern for PML. The critical diagnostic clue emerges only on follow-up testing (repeat LP, PCR panel, blood cultures).
metadata.difficulty_rationale: 5 required tools; 3 red herrings; immunocompromise produces pauci-cellular or atypical CSF response
metadata.revision_reason: Reviewer 2 meningitis audit: complete LP/microbiology/lab pathway, no ECG, and MRI restricted to complications or non-response

patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. Okonkwo is a 42-year-old right-handed man with known HIV infection diagnosed three years ago who presents to the emergency department with a one-day history of worsening headache, confusion, restlessness, and left-sided chest pain. He was hospitalized two months prior at an outside facility for a similar presentation of headache and altered mental status, where he was treated empirically with intravenous ceftriaxone for presumed bacterial meningitis and high-dose fluconazole for possible cryptococcal meningitis. At that time, he was also initiated on antiretroviral therapy with tenofovir, lamivudine, and efavirenz, along with co-trimoxazole prophylaxis. His CD4 count at the prior admission was 359 cells per cubic millimeter. He reports partial improvement after the initial hospitalization and was discharged with instructions to continue his antiretroviral regimen and fluconazole prophylaxis.

Over the past two weeks, his wife has noticed progressive changes in his behavior, including increased irritability, occasional episodes of inappropriate laughter, and difficulty with everyday tasks that he previously performed without difficulty. He has been sleeping poorly and appears restless at night. Three days ago, he developed a dull, diffuse headache that has gradually worsened. Yesterday, he became noticeably confused, unable to recall recent conversations, and more agitated than usual. His wife brought him to the emergency department today after he complained of sharp left-sided chest pain and appeared increasingly disoriented.

The patient reports that he has had a persistent ulcer on the inside of his right cheek near the molar area for approximately three weeks. He has not sought dental care for this lesion and has been managing it with saltwater rinses. He also notes intermittent mild left jaw swelling that he attributes to bruxism during sleep. He denies any recent fever, though his wife recalls that he felt warm to the touch during his prior hospitalization. He denies cough, shortness of breath at rest, abdominal pain, urinary symptoms, rash, or joint pains. He has been adherent to his antiretroviral medications and co-trimoxazole but admits he occasionally forgets the fluconazole.

His prior meningitis workup at the outside hospital was reportedly negative for cryptococcal antigen and tuberculosis, though detailed records are not available. He has no history of seizures, but his wife describes two brief episodes over the past week where he appeared to stare blankly and his arms stiffened for approximately 30 seconds before returning to baseline, which she attributed to fatigue. He has not had any witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizures. He has not traveled outside his usual routes in the past six months and has no known sick contacts with tuberculosis.

neurological_exam.additional: Nuchal rigidity present with resistance to passive neck flexion. Kernig sign positive bilaterally. Brudzinski sign positive. No rash, petechiae, or purpura on full skin examination. An ulcerated lesion approximately 1.5 cm in diameter noted on the right buccal mucosa near the molar region, present for approximately 3 weeks per patient report. A firm, mildly tender left submandibular lymph node approximately 2 cm in diameter is palpated. Mild left-sided jaw swelling noted, patient attributes to biting his cheek during a recent episode of teeth clenching at night.

Hearing grossly intact bilaterally. Palate elevates symmetrically. Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength 5/5 bilaterally. Tongue midline without fasciculations.
neurological_exam.gait: Gait steady with normal base and arm swing. Tandem gait intact. Romberg negative.
